h1:
Ubon Nature Trip Along the Mekong
Pha Taem, Sam Phan Bok & Saeng Chan Falls
intro: The eastern edge of Ubon that hugs the Mekong is where nature has been hard at work for millions of years — Sam Phan Bok, where the water has carved thousands of potholes into the rock; Pha Taem, with prehistoric rock paintings over three thousand years old; and Saeng Chan Waterfall, the only falls in Thailand that pours through a hole in the rock. For this 3-day, 2-night plan we have you stay out near Khong Chiam and Pho Sai so you are not driving back to the city every day. We have checked the opening hours, entry fees and best season for every spot, because some of them look completely different from one month to the next.

blocks.html: The first thing to understand before planning a Ubon nature trip is that the season decides what you actually see. Sam Phan Bok looks best when the water is low — late winter into the hot season (roughly December to May) — because the rock potholes are exposed and you can walk among them. Saeng Chan Waterfall is the opposite: you need the rainy season into early winter (October to January) for a proper flow through the rock hole. The sweet spot for catching almost everything is the late-rains/early-winter window, around November to December — the weather is good, the waterfall still has water, and Sam Phan Bok is starting to dry out. The two-colour river (the chalky Mekong meeting the indigo Mun) is sharpest in the dry season, around March to May.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Into Khong Chiam, Pha Taem and the two-colour river

blocks.html: It is about 80 km from Ubon city to Khong Chiam, an hour and a half by car. On the first day we cover the southern side of Pha Taem National Park first — both the rock paintings and the mushroom rocks — then come down to stay near Khong Chiam to catch the two-colour river in the evening.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Ubon city → Pha Taem → Sao Chaliang → two-colour river, Khong Chiam

items.activity: Leave Ubon city heading toward Khong Chiam district. Stop to fill up the tank and grab enough water for the car.
items.note: About 80 km, around 1.5 hours · shops are sparse inside the park, so bring water and snacks with you.

items.activity: Enter Pha Taem National Park to see the prehistoric rock paintings, roughly 3,000–4,000 years old, on the cliff face above the Mekong. Walk the trail down to the paintings, then loop back up to the viewpoint.
items.note: Open 05:00–18:00 daily · entry 40 THB for Thai adults, 20 THB for children · the path down is a stone staircase, so trainers are more comfortable · Huai Phai subdistrict, Khong Chiam.

items.activity: Stop at Sao Chaliang, the mushroom-shaped rock pillars carved by wind and water over millions of years, just a little before the park headquarters. They photograph well at any time of day.
items.note: Same park, no extra entry fee · the midday sun is strong, so bring a hat and umbrella.

items.activity: Head down for lunch in Khong Chiam town. Pick a riverside place that cooks Mekong river fish — tom yum giant catfish, grilled fish or fish laap.
items.note: Fresh Mekong river fish is the local highlight; prices go by fish size, so ordering shared dishes works out better value.

items.activity: Check in to your stay around Khong Chiam. Somewhere right on the river or near the two-colour river viewpoint is handy. Drop your bags and rest a while to escape the afternoon heat.
items.note: Riverside places in Khong Chiam range from small resorts to homestays. Book ahead in the cool season because it gets busy.

items.activity: Go to the two-colour river viewpoint, where the indigo Mun River meets the chalky, silty Mekong. On a clear day you can see the line between the two distinctly. Sit and enjoy the cool breeze.
items.note: The two colours are sharpest in the dry season (Mar–May) · in the rainy season both run muddy and the line is faint · you can take a boat out for a closer look at a price agreed with the boat owner.

items.activity: Have an easy dinner at a café or riverside spot in Khong Chiam, sipping a drink as the sun sets behind the river.
items.note: Riverside cafés like Mong Khong Cafe & Camping and Khwam Song Cham have coffee, desserts and simple food. Drinks start around 60 THB.

blocks.title: About where to stay
blocks.html: If you want to fit both Sam Phan Bok and Pha Chana Dai into one trip, we suggest the first night in Khong Chiam, then for the second night either shift over toward Pho Sai or come back to Khong Chiam — your call. Sam Phan Bok is in a different district from Saeng Chan Waterfall, so a little looping saves more time than driving back to the city every day.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Sam Phan Bok, the Grand Canyon of Thailand

blocks.html: Sam Phan Bok is a rocky shoal in the middle of the Mekong where the water has carved out thousands of potholes ("bok" in the local dialect), exposed for walking only when the water is low. It sits in Pho Sai district, about an hour-plus drive north from Khong Chiam along the river. We set out a bit early today, because walking on bare rock in full sun gets brutal if you leave it late.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Hat Salueng → boat to Sam Phan Bok → rock formations → back to your stay in the evening

items.activity: Leave Khong Chiam and drive along the Mekong toward Pho Sai district. Grab breakfast on the way or pack a box to eat at the beach.
items.note: The riverside road has lovely views but is narrow in places, so drive carefully · leaving early lets you walk Sam Phan Bok before the sun gets harsh.

items.activity: Reach Hat Salueng at Ban Pak Kalang, Song Khon subdistrict — the boat launch for Sam Phan Bok. It is a white sand beach over 800 metres long on the Mekong. Have a wander and some photos before boarding.
items.note: Hat Salueng is the main boat launch · a chartered boat is priced by agreement with the owner, depending on group size and stops; going as a larger group brings the per-person cost down.

items.activity: Take the boat down the Mekong from Hat Salueng to Sam Phan Bok, about 4 km. Along the way you pass rock formations people have given playful names, like the dog's head rock and Pak Bong.
items.note: In the low-water season (Dec–May) the potholes are clearly exposed and you can walk on the rock ridges · in the rainy season the water floods the bok, so you can cruise by boat but not walk.

items.activity: Climb up and explore Sam Phan Bok on foot — the dog's head rock, the angel's vase, and the round water-carved holes that look almost sculpted. You can easily spend an hour walking and shooting photos.
items.note: Some rock is slippery and gets hot later in the morning, so tread carefully and carry enough water · there is no shade, so wear a hat and sunglasses.

items.activity: Head back to shore at Hat Salueng and break for lunch at a beachside place or in Pho Sai town. Isan food and river fish are the mainstays.
items.note: Places around Hat Salueng open with the tourist season; on a weekday off-season there may be fewer open, so have a backup in town.

items.activity: Stop at Hat Chom Dao or a Mekong viewpoint on the way back. Some spots have coloured rock terraces and a lovely view of the river's bend, good for photos in the late afternoon.
items.note: If you are worn out from Sam Phan Bok, you can skip this and head back to rest — no need to push it.

items.activity: Return to your stay in Khong Chiam, shower and rest, then head out for an unhurried riverside dinner.
items.note: Today involves a lot of walking in strong sun, so leave time to let your body recover before the final day.

blocks.title: Season is the key
blocks.html: Do not expect to walk Sam Phan Bok if you come in the rainy season (Jun–Oct), because the Mekong runs high and floods all the bok. During that time you can cruise by boat to look, but you cannot walk on the rock. If you are set on walking the bok, pick December to May — the closer to the hot season, the lower the water and the more potholes you will see.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Saeng Chan Waterfall and last odds and ends before heading home

blocks.html: The last day is for Saeng Chan Waterfall, also called the "falls through a hole" — water that flows down through a single hole in the rock as one stream, the only one of its kind in Thailand. It is at Ban Thung Na Muang, Na Pho Klang subdistrict, also within Pha Taem National Park. If you are an early riser, you can get up to watch the sunrise at Pha Chana Dai first, since it is the spot where the sun rises before anywhere else in Siam.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: (optional) Pha Chana Dai → Saeng Chan Waterfall → back to Ubon city

items.activity: (For the early-rising crowd) Drive to Pha Chana Dai, the spot where the sun rises before anywhere else in Siam, and catch first light over the Mekong and the Lao bank.
items.note: It is at the far eastern tip of Pha Taem National Park; the access road is fairly far and rough, so check road conditions with the rangers first · if it is not for you, skip this and sleep in.

items.activity: Have breakfast, pack up and check out, then head for Saeng Chan Waterfall at Ban Thung Na Muang.
items.note: The waterfall is within Pha Taem National Park, so if you bought a park ticket on day one, ask the rangers about reusing it.

items.activity: Walk down to Saeng Chan Waterfall to see the stream flowing through the rock hole like a curtain of moonlight. Below the falls there is a spot to shoot upward and catch the water threading through the hole.
items.note: Best in the rainy season into early winter (Oct–Jan), when there is plenty of water · in the dry season the flow is thin to dry and you may only see the rock hole · the path down is stone and can be slippery.

items.activity: If you still have time, stop at the nearby Thung Na Muang Waterfall, or settle into a riverside café for one last coffee before you go.
items.note: Several riverside cafés have a signature drink named after the two-colour river — worth ordering for a photo before you leave.

items.activity: Have a final lunch in Khong Chiam, then drive back to Ubon city. You can pick up souvenirs along the way.
items.note: You will be back in the city around three or four in the afternoon, so leave enough time to return a rental car or get to Ubon airport.

blocks.text: Getting there and what to prepare

items: Your own car is easiest — the sights are spread across Khong Chiam and Pho Sai, and public transport is hard to reach them with. If you fly into Ubon airport and rent a car to drive yourself, you will move around most freely.
No car? You can charter a tour or local van — there are 2-day, 1-night Sam Phan Bok–Pha Taem tours out of Ubon city that include the boat and a guide, good if you would rather not drive.
Bring water and snacks — shops are sparse inside the park and out at Sam Phan Bok, and the sun is strong, so always carry enough water.
Trainers + hat + sunscreen — all three spots involve walking on rock in full sun. Sandals slip easily, especially at the waterfall and Sam Phan Bok.
Check the season before booking — Sam Phan Bok is walkable when the water is low, Saeng Chan Waterfall is best in the rains. Plan your dates around what you most want to see.

blocks.text: What to eat along the Mekong

blocks.html: The highlight around Khong Chiam and Pho Sai is fresh Mekong river fish — giant catfish, sheatfish and river prawns. Most riverside places cook them as tom yum, grilled fish or laap, eaten with sticky rice and jaew dipping sauce. For the café crowd, there are spots with river views where you can sit, sip coffee and watch the sunset.

items.name: Riverside restaurant, Khong Chiam
items.blurb: A local home-style restaurant on the river, focused on Mekong river fish, small shrimp and river prawns, right by the water — a good fit for lunch on day one.

items.name: Mong Khong Cafe & Camping
items.blurb: A café right on the Mekong with drinks, desserts, Thai–Isan–Western food and a camping zone. Drinks start around 60 THB, with a panoramic river view.

items.name: Khwam Song Cham Cafe
items.blurb: A laid-back riverside café with house-roasted coffee, well-priced cakes and a savoury menu too, where you can sit and watch the river for a good long while — a fine last cup before heading home.

faq.q: What month should I visit Ubon for nature?
faq.a: It depends on what you want to see. You can walk on the rock potholes at Sam Phan Bok when the water is low, which is December to May. Saeng Chan Waterfall is at its best when there is plenty of water, which is October to January. The window where you can catch almost everything with good weather is late rains into early winter, around November to December.

faq.q: Can you visit Sam Phan Bok in the rainy season?
faq.a: You can, but you won't be able to walk on the bok, because in the rainy season (June to October) the Mekong runs high and floods all the rock holes. During that time you can cruise the river by boat but cannot get out to explore the rock on foot. If you mean to come and walk the bok, choose the low-water season.

faq.q: What time does Pha Taem open and how much is entry?
faq.a: Pha Taem National Park is open 05:00 to 18:00 daily. Entry is 40 THB for Thai adults and 20 THB for children. It opens very early because it is also a sunrise spot. Within the park you'll find the rock paintings, Sao Chaliang and Saeng Chan Waterfall.

faq.q: Can you do this route without your own car?
faq.a: You can, but it is a bit of a hassle, because the sights are spread out and public transport struggles to reach them. The easier option is to charter a van with a driver from Ubon city, or buy a 2-day, 1-night Sam Phan Bok–Pha Taem tour that already includes the boat and a guide.

faq.q: Where do you see the two-colour river and when is it clearest?
faq.a: You see it in Khong Chiam district, at the point where the indigo Mun River meets the chalky, silty Mekong. The colour line is sharpest in the dry season, around March to May, and on a clear day. You can take a boat out for a closer look at a price agreed with the boat owner.
